title: "Exercises — Amplification"
---

Pen and paper. Try each one before opening the **Hint**, and the hint before the
**Solution** — the reasoning is the point, not the answer.

Have the [NEB selection charts](https://www.neb.com/en/tools-and-resources/selection-charts)
open for the enzyme questions.

# Part 1 — PCR

## E1. Errors and cycles

A 300 bp amplicon is made in 15 cycles. Take the error rate as 10^-5 per base per doubling for a
proofreading enzyme and 10^-4 for one without proofreading (illustrative values; read your own
datasheet). The mean number of errors per final molecule is approximately rate x length x
doublings / 2.

a. What fraction of molecules carries an error with each enzyme (treat the mean as a probability)?
b. Is a change from 15 to 10 cycles or a change of enzyme worth more?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
The factor 2 is there because half of the strands in the final pool are the original templates.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. Proofreading: 10^-5 x 300 x 15 / 2 = 0.0225, about **2 %**. Without proofreading: 10 times
   that, **22 %** (and the approximation starts to break down, since a molecule can carry more
   than one error).
b. Ten cycles instead of 15 cuts the proofreading figure by a third (to 1.5 %). The enzyme change
   cuts it ten-fold. Both help; the enzyme is the larger lever, but cycles are free and also
   reduce bias, duplicates and chimeras.
:::

## E2. The cycle budget

You have 5 ng of fragmented human DNA. Adapter ligation converts about 25 % of it into amplifiable
library, and you want 100 ng. Each cycle multiplies by (1 + E).

a. How many cycles at E = 0.9?
b. How many at E = 0.7?
c. Which result tells you to be more careful with the reaction?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Library after ligation: 0.25 x 5 = 1.25 ng, so the required gain is 100 / 1.25 = 80.
a. ln 80 / ln 1.9 = 4.38 / 0.642 = 6.8, so **7 cycles**.
b. ln 80 / ln 1.7 = 4.38 / 0.531 = 8.3, so **8 or 9 cycles**.
c. The second: inhibitors or poor primer design make you take more cycles, and each extra
   cycle brings more bias and more duplicates. A drop in efficiency is itself a signal to
   investigate.
:::

## E3. Saturation

A library has 20 million distinct molecules. Expected distinct reads from M reads is
N(1 - e^(-M/N)).

a. How many distinct reads, and what duplicate fraction, from 40 million reads?
b. What do you gain by doubling to 80 million reads?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. 20 x (1 - e^-2) = 20 x 0.865 = **17.3 million** distinct. Duplicate fraction:
   1 - 17.3/40 = **57 %**.
b. 20 x (1 - e^-4) = 19.6 million distinct, a gain of 2.3 million for 40 million more reads. More
   sequencing cannot fix a library that is already exhausted: you need more input molecules.
:::

## E4. A bubble

Your library has a fluorometric concentration that looks fine but a qPCR concentration far lower.
The trace shows the peak at about 800 bp, although the inserts are 400 bp. You used 20 cycles from 1 ng.
What happened, and what do you do?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Which assay counts molecules that have both adapter ends fully double-stranded?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
The PCR ran past the plateau. Products of different inserts annealed through their shared adapters
and made bubble heteroduplexes, which migrate slower (so 800 bp) and have unpaired single-strand
regions that fluorescence counts but that do not amplify well in qPCR or cluster. Fix: re-amplify
with one cycle in fresh master mix to convert the heteroduplexes to duplex, and start again with
fewer cycles or more input.
:::

# Part 2 — Other ways to copy

## E5. Choose the amplification

Pick one method for each case, and name the property that decides it.

a. Variants in a single human cell, called with high specificity
b. Where did a lentiviral vector integrate in a transduced human cell line?
c. Detecting a virus in saliva in a place with no thermal cycler
d. A 16.6 kb human mitochondrial genome from 1 ng of DNA, on a short-read machine
e. Transcriptome from 200 cells where relative abundance matters more than length

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. **PTA** (or MALBAC): copies stay primary, so false variants from copy-of-copy errors are
   fewer than with MDA.
b. **LAM-PCR, inverse PCR or splinkerette PCR**: each reads from the known vector end into the
   unknown flank.
c. **LAMP**: isothermal, one temperature, visual or simple readout.
d. **Tiled multiplex amplicons in two pools**: overlapping products cover the whole genome and
   adjacent amplicons never share a tube.
e. **IVT-based linear amplification** (for example CEL-seq): each RNA is copied from the
   original, so abundance is preserved.
:::

## E6. Why linear keeps ratios

Two transcripts, A and B, are present at 10:1. Amplification efficiency is 90 % for A and 80 % for B.

a. After 20 PCR cycles, what is the ratio?
b. Under linear amplification in which each template produces 100 copies, give or take 10 %, what
   is the largest distortion you can expect?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. The ratio is multiplied by (1.9 / 1.8)^20 = 1.0556^20 ≈ 2.95. A:B becomes about **30 : 1**.
b. The copy number varies at most 10 % either way, so the ratio is distorted by at most about
   1.1 / 0.9 = 1.2-fold, and it does not compound with cycles.
:::

## E7. Designing an inverse PCR

You know 600 bp of a lentiviral vector and want to map its integration sites in human cells.

a. What must be true of the enzyme you digest with?
b. A 4-cutter cuts about every 256 bp; a 6-cutter every 4 096 bp. What does each do to the
   circle you make?
c. Why is the ligation done in a large volume?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Think about what is the largest circle PCR can handle, and what a circle of 100 bp looks like to a polymerase.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. It must not cut between the two primer sites inside the known sequence, so the primers stay on one
   fragment, and it should cut near the junction on at least the unknown side. Check the vector
   sequence with the NEB charts.
b. A 4-cutter gives circles of a few hundred bases or fewer: some are too small to close, and the
   product holds little flank. A 6-cutter gives circles of several kb, which may be too long to amplify
   well and are often outside what the polymerase handles easily. Many protocols use a 4- or 5-base
   enzyme with a long-range polymerase, or two digests in parallel.
c. Dilution favours the fragment joining to its own other end (intramolecular), rather than to
   another fragment, which would give concatemers and chimeric junctions.
:::

## E8. The phosphate on a splinkerette

A splinkerette adapter is supplied without a 5'-phosphate on its hairpin strand, and a colleague
phosphorylates it to improve ligation efficiency. Predict the effect.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Which strand of the adapter ligates to the genomic fragment when it is unphosphorylated, and
which does not?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Without a phosphate, only the recessed strand ligates to the genomic 5' phosphate; the hairpin
strand stays nicked from the genomic 3' end. The adapter primer site therefore appears only after
a vector-specific primer has copied through the junction. A phosphorylated adapter lets the
hairpin strand ligate too, so the primer site is present on the original strand, and every
fragment with adapters becomes a template for the adapter primer: the one-sided background the
design was supposed to prevent returns. (This follows the logic of the published design; check the
protocol notes for the sequences.)
:::

## E9. Droplets

An emulsion PCR makes droplets that each contain one bead. The templates are Poisson distributed
with mean lambda per droplet. P(0) = e^-lambda, P(1) = lambda e^-lambda.

a. For lambda = 0.1, what share of droplets that contain any template contain more than one?
b. The same for lambda = 1.
c. Why not choose lambda = 0.01?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. P(0) = 0.905, P(1) = 0.0905, P(2 or more) = 1 - 0.905 - 0.0905 = 0.0047. Among occupied
   droplets: 0.0047 / 0.0952 = **4.9 %** mixed.
b. P(0) = 0.368, P(1) = 0.368, P(2 or more) = 0.264. Among occupied: 0.264 / 0.632 = **42 %**
   mixed.
c. At 0.01 only about 1 % of beads carry any DNA, so almost all the capacity of the emulsion is
   wasted. The choice is a balance, and beads with DNA can be enriched afterwards.
:::

## E10. Consensus from a circle

Each read of a base is wrong with probability p = 10^-3, independently. A rolling-circle product
gives three reads of the same base.

a. What is the chance that the majority (at least 2 of 3) is wrong?
b. Which errors does this not remove?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. 3 p^2 (1 - p) + p^3 ≈ 3 x 10^-6, a reduction of about 300-fold from 10^-3.
b. Errors made when the circle itself was first copied, and in the first round of rolling-circle
   synthesis, which are present in every repeat. Also damage in the original molecule. Consensus
   removes independent errors only.
:::

## E11. Uracil and the polymerase

Your USER-adapter library is amplified with a proofreading polymerase of the Pfu type, and nothing
amplifies. The adapter U was not cut because the USER enzyme was left out by mistake. Explain and
suggest two fixes.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Family B proofreading polymerases stall on uracil in the template, so the strand carrying the
adapter uracil is not copied. Fixes: treat with USER (uracil excision) before PCR, as the protocol
intends, or amplify with a uracil-tolerant polymerase listed as such on the datasheet.
:::

# Self-check

Answer without looking anything up.

1. Why does an error in an early cycle matter more than one in a late cycle?
2. What causes the plateau in PCR?
3. Why does an over-amplified library run high on a gel?
4. Which amplifications do not copy from copies?
5. How does a nested PCR reject mispriming products?
6. Why is the splinkerette adapter hairpin-shaped?
7. Why does an emulsion not use a high template concentration?
8. What errors can rolling-circle consensus not remove?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answers
1. The error is copied into all descendants, so it reaches a bigger share of the final pool.
2. Primers and polymerase are used up, and products reanneal to each other instead.
3. Bubble heteroduplexes form between different molecules that share adapter ends.
4. IVT and single-primer linear amplification, and in a looser sense PTA, where terminators keep
   the copies primary.
5. Wrong products rarely carry the inner primer sites.
6. Its primer site is created only by a copy running through from the vector-specific primer.
7. Many droplets would hold two or more templates, and the beads would be mixed.
8. Errors in the first copy of the circle and damage in the original molecule.
:::

# Going further

- Take a PCR recipe you use and compute the maximum number of molecules it can make before primers
  run out. How far from the plateau are you at your normal cycle number?
- Find the polymerase in your lab freezer and record its fidelity, uracil tolerance and
  strand-displacement activity from the datasheet.
